title: after summer wildfires record heat americans are talking about climate change  ecmii 2026 09 08
author: John Marshall
text:
September 7 - A World Cup final played under the haze of wildfire smoke. A World Cup final played under the haze of wildfire smoke. Fourth of July parades cancelled due to extreme heat. In Washington, half a million acres burned in just a couple months of wildfire season, almost double last year’s total. Seventeen states under an emergency electricity order. Record-breaking temperatures from Atlantic City, New Jersey to Miles City, Montana, where it reached 115 degrees while over 180 million Americans – nearly half the population – were placed under major heat alerts due to a “life-threatening heat dome”.
Yet American leaders are dangerously quiet about climate change. Some, of course, are actively antagonistic. But even those who may, on paper, support action hesitate to address the problem directly. An analysis of press releases issued by members of the House and Senate shows that mentions of climate change have plummeted since 2025, a large-scale “climate hushing” driven by a spreading perception that climate change is a losing issue with the American public.
I am the founder ​of a climate education nonprofit, Potential Energy Coalition, and our data disagrees. For nearly a decade, we’ve spent thousands of hours in focus groups, surveyed over half-a-million people, and tested ​hundreds of messages, all in an effort to understand how people feel about climate change and how they respond to climate change narratives. Our ⁠research makes one thing very clear: not only is our current “climate hushing” disheartening and dangerous, it’s also bad strategy. Climate change is not a losing issue, and the majority of Americans want their ​leaders to act on it.
It’s been a smoky, simmering summer, and the public is feeling it. Seventy percent of Americans report experiencing at least one extreme weather impact in the past year, from ​multi-day power outages and cancelled outdoor plans to being trapped indoors avoiding toxic air. Data from a new AP-NORC poll shows how fast these personal impacts are rising: 80% of Americans now say extreme heat has increased their electric bills (up from 69% two years ago) and 68% say it limits outdoor activities (up from 57%).
Not surprisingly, then, people are also talking about it. According to data from Potential Energy’s social listening tool, which analyzes conversation from ​over a dozen different social channels, the conversation around extreme heat, wildfires and droughts this summer has increased 103% from the same period last year, and posts that explicitly connect extreme weather with ​climate change have increased by 263%.
Europe, too, has had a “summer of reckoning,” but leaders like Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez are unafraid to connect the dots: “What we are experiencing is not a series of isolated incidents. It is the consequence of a climate emergency that is making wildfires even more violent, heat waves more frequent.”
Americans want to hear more from their own leaders. In fact, 65% agreed with the simple, emphatic statement: “If public officials won’t acknowledge climate change is happening, they’re putting lives and livelihoods at risk.” Some leaders worry that talking about climate change in the midst of an extreme weather emergency is “politicizing a tragedy”, but when we proposed that theory to Americans, two in three did not agree. Far more agreed with the statement, “We can’t truly prepare for extreme weather if we aren’t willing to talk about ​climate change.”
Other communicators think it’s better to go ​through the “side door” by selling the benefits ⁠of climate change solutions (such as clean jobs or energy affordability) rather than talking directly about climate change. This, too, turned out to be false. Our latest research in partnership with the Rockefeller foundation, showed “front door” messages that directly name the human, material consequences (such as rising insurance premiums, worsening pollution and ​dangerous heat) are 2.6 times as effective at increasing support as messages that attempt to sell “side-door” benefits, which often feel abstract and distant ​from everyday life. When you ⁠talk about the consequences Americans are already feeling, the numbers move.
More than talk, though, Americans want action. Nearly 70% of Americans support government action on climate change. Two in three say officials haven’t done enough to prepare us for extreme weather, including 73% of moderates and half of conservatives. What does that preparation look like? Six in 10 agree that policies to reduce fossil fuel use will help prevent worsening ⁠extreme weather; ​only 17% disagree. On climate change, the public isn’t nearly as polarized as the politicians.
Americans want more clean energy and ​less of the fossil fuel pollution that’s overheating the planet. It’s time for climate-friendly leaders to get back on the offense, push back against today’s dangerous rollbacks, and stop avoiding an issue that the majority of Americans are increasingly worried ​about.
Nature is talking. Politicians are not. What we need isn’t a massive shying away from the issue, but leaders ready to talk about the consequences we’re all feeling, with plans to start fixing them.
